en: Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty, recorded by his disciple Guanding.

Next, regarding the sixth [stage], the practice of giving through contemplation: one contemplates before the thought of giving arises, while about to give, while in the act of giving, and after having given.
Thus, the slowness or speed of the four movements is entirely unapprehendable,
nor is this unapprehensibility itself perceived.
Upon turning back to observe the awakened mind, one finds it does not come from without;
it does not go out from within, nor does it arise from between.
It does not possess self-existence as a constant entity.
Non-action and the non-actor are ultimately empty and quiescent;
yet, because the mind exerts its influence, there is coming and going,
whether for the sake of violating precepts or deceiving others.
Either to serve as a retinue or to surpass others;
either for the sake of yielding to a superior or for the sake of virtuous meditation;
either for the sake of nirvana or for the sake of compassion.
Abandoning the six sense objects and setting the six modes of action in motion,
one employs skillful means such that coming and going, lifting the foot and setting it down, are all like illusions and transformations.
In this state of vast emptiness, both subject and object suddenly vanish.
A road of a thousand li is not said to be remote;
a space of a few steps is not said to be near.
In all that one undertakes, one’s efforts shall not be in vain.
Without expecting any recompense,
one thus abides in giving to encompass and accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
endowed with the Mahāyāna, one is able to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, one observes that a single movement of the mind is fully endowed with ten dharmas.
Because the one is not fixed as one, it can become ten;
because the ten are not fixed as ten, they can become one.
Neither one nor ten, yet illuminating both one and ten simultaneously;
within a single thought-moment, the three truths are fully present.
Whether standing, sitting, reclining, speaking, remaining silent, acting, or non-acting.
It is also thus; it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
Furthermore, it is seen that sons of the Buddha give away fine robes and superior garments as alms in order to seek the Buddha-way;
this is precisely what is meant by this principle.
Previously, the six [perfections] were discussed collectively with respect to twelve matters;
now, they are discussed individually with respect to each matter.
When a practitioner practices, they observe sentient beings with the eye of great compassion.
Not perceiving the mark of a sentient being,
and causing sentient beings to attain fearlessness toward the bodhisattva—
this is the perfection of giving within practice.
To cause no harm to sentient beings and to perceive neither the signs of sin nor merit—
this is called *śīla*.
When acting, one’s thoughts and mental conceptions do not arise.
Furthermore, it is without movement and has no place of abiding;
the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are likewise entirely unmoving.
This is called patience.
When walking, one must not lift or set down the feet with deliberate thought;
the mind has no prior intention or subsequent awareness.
Among all phenomena, there is no arising, abiding, or ceasing.
This is called diligence.
It does not apprehend body or mind, nor birth-and-death or nirvana.
Among all phenomena, there is no grasping, mindfulness, or attachment; it is without relish and without distraction.
This is called dhyāna.
When practicing, the six parts of the body, such as the head and so forth, are like clouds, shadows, dreams, illusions, echoes, and transformations;
they are without arising or ceasing, and without annihilation or permanence.
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases are empty and quiescent, neither bound nor liberated;
this is called prajñā.
This is explained in detail, as in the Śūraṅgama [Sūtra].
Furthermore, within the midst of practice there is a state of stillness characterized by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If one does not examine this, defiled greed will arise toward that concentration, and one will become attached to the flavor of dhyāna.
Now, observe the mind of concentration.
Since the mind itself is non-existent, where could concentration abide?
One should know that this concentration arises from inversion.
When observing in this way, one perceives neither emptiness nor non-emptiness.
Thus, by breaking through fixed characteristics, one does not give rise to greedy attachment;
this is the understanding of the bodhisattva produced through skillful means.
A practitioner who has not yet realized this may instead conceive the thought, "I am able to observe the mind."
This refers to subtle wisdom.
To be attached to this wisdom and to exalt oneself on its account is called the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Like those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one will not attain liberation.
One then reflects back upon the observing mind and finds no place of abiding, nor any arising or ceasing.
Ultimately, there is neither an observer nor a non-observer.
Since the observer is absent, [the observed is likewise absent].
Whoever contemplates all phenomena and does not apprehend the contemplation of the mind is immediately free from conceptualization.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
When conceptualization and observation have been eliminated and the mind of frivolous proliferation is entirely extinguished,
immeasurable multitudes of sins are removed and the pure mind is ever unified.
A person of such noble and wondrous character is then able to perceive Prajñā.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* says:
"To contemplate the mind within the mind" refers precisely to this intention.
Within these practices, one possesses the three samādhis.
First, by observing and shattering all various marks of existence (*nimitta*), one does not perceive either the internal or the external;
this is the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Next, one contemplates the characteristic of emptiness that can destroy [phenomena];
this is called the samādhi of signlessness (animitta-samādhi).
Finally, one contemplates the non-perception of an agent; this is the samādhi of wishlessness (apraṇihita-samādhi).
Furthermore, one destroys the three inversions and the three poisons, transcends the flow of the three realms of existence,
subdues the four maras and their enmity,
accomplishes the pāramitās, embraces the dharma-realm, and increases and fulfills all dharma-gates.
How could it be limited merely to the six perfections and the three samādhis?
If one is fully endowed with all dharmas within their practice,
the same applies to the other eleven matters as well.
Next, they further passed through the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), vying with one another to maintain the utmost care and purity,
like one holding an oil bowl without spilling even a single drop.
Furthermore, regarding the six activities (*ṣatkarma*):
Their deportment is solemn and their advances and retreats are orderly;
this is merely called "observing the precepts.
The karmic fruit of observing the precepts is to ascend and emerge to receive happiness.
It is not that this samādhi is not called a pāramitā;
rather, if one attains the wisdom of contemplation regarding the twelve matters, the śīla is spontaneously perfected.
That is to say, one contemplates the four movements of the mind regarding form (*rūpa*) that has not yet been seen, the desire to see it, the seeing of it, and having already seen it.
Through various investigations, one cannot find the mind that arises, nor can one find the mind that contemplates.

It is neither internal nor external, without coming or going, tranquil, and devoid of arising or ceasing. When one is able to contemplate in this way, the seven branches of body and speech are as pure as space.
This is to maintain the threefold discipline of precepts that are unimpaired, unbroken, and unpierced;
by destroying the various evil thoughts and observations of the four modes of activity,
one maintains the precept of non-confusion.
Not being disturbed by the four movements of the mind is precisely to maintain the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus,
the four movements of the mind do not arise.
This is precisely upholding the precepts associated with the Path.
To discern the various four modes of activity without obstruction is precisely upholding the precept of non-attachment.
To discern the four modes of activity without error is precisely to uphold the precepts praised by the wise.
To know that these four modes encompass all phenomena is [the essence of such upholding].
This is precisely upholding the sovereign precepts of the Mahāyāna.
By recognizing the four movements and the four virtues, one upholds the ultimate precepts; when these two minds are clear and pure, both extremes are simultaneously negated.
Entering correctly into the Middle Way, one simultaneously illuminates the two truths;
this is the inconceivable realm of the Buddha, complete and without deficiency. Regarding its three aspects, the "aspected" (rūpa) and the "experiencer" (vedaka) are both unapprehendable.
When these three matters are all absent, that is *dāna* (generosity).
To settle the mind unmoving amidst each and every form is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To be without defilement or interruption amidst each and every form is called *vīrya* (diligence).
Not being disturbed by the various forms of form is called dhyāna.
That the various forms of form are like illusions and like transformations is called prajñā.
That the various forms of form are like space is called the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi).
Not apprehending this emptiness is called the samādhi of signlessness;
having neither subject nor object is called the samādhi of wishlessness.
How could it be limited to the three truths, the six perfections, and the three kinds of emptiness?
All the Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, can be understood by analogy with this.
Just as it is with the sense-object of form (*rūpa*),
so it is with the other five sense-objects.
The same applies to the six sensations and the six activities.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha, fully endowed with dignified deportment, seeking the path of the Buddha."
This is precisely that meaning.
Next, regarding the successive stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and goodness (*śubha*),
one again considers both the performing and the experiencing [of karma] in terms of their opposition and conformity.
That which is agreeable is pleasant;
that which is disagreeable is unpleasant.
One does not feel anger toward the disagreeable, nor does one feel attachment toward the agreeable.
There is no seeing and no seer;
there is no action and no agent—
all as explained above.
Next is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
The old [translation] states:
"Diligence has no separate essence; it is simply the earnest application toward all practices."
Inferring from this principle, there ought to be a distinct entity;
for example, while ignorance (*avidyā*) is included among the various proclivities (*anuśaya*), there is yet another distinct ignorance.
For now, let us rely on the *Sūtra on the Recitation of the Precepts* to diligently exert the mind.
One should apply oneself with diligence,
practicing day and night without fail until it becomes smooth and supple;
yet this is not yet the wisdom of samādhi.
Now, observing that the breath touches seven locations and their conjunction produces sound like an echo—
neither internal nor external, with neither a reciter nor a recitation—
one thoroughly investigates this by means of the four modes of analysis.
One who does not give rise to sensation regarding sensory objects,
one who does not produce an agent regarding conditions,
and one whose afflictions do not interrupt their recitation and exposition.
"Thought after thought, one flows into the great ocean of *nirvāṇa*.
This is called diligence," and so forth.
Next, he passes through the various *dhyānas*.
The fundamental nine notions, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth,
are merely meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and not perfections (*pāramitā*).
Even when observing the four phases of entering meditative absorption, one does not perceive the mind.
Wherever there is concentration,
one immediately penetrates the true reality of dhyāna;
through dhyāna, one encompasses all phenomena.
Therefore, the fifth chapter of the treatise concludes the explanation of the eight perceptions and elucidates the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all dharmas.
Yet, the various masters of the treatises do not grasp its profound intent.
All [the critics] claim that the treatise is erroneous and should not have stated this.
However, this is because the Master of the Treatise clarifies the characteristics of the Mahāyāna through the eight perceptions;
therefore, he provides an extensive explanation of all phenomena, and so forth.
Next, regarding the one who traverses through wisdom:
the Commentary explains the eightfold understanding of *prajñā*.
For now, we shall briefly apply worldly wisdom to contemplate the six feelings and the six formations.
The four modes of movement cannot be apprehended by worldly wisdom;
this is as explained above.
This applies likewise to all other wholesome dharmas.
Question:
If a single dharma encompasses all dharmas,
then the mere practice of contemplation would suffice.
What need is there to employ cessation?
One instance is sufficient;
why employ five instances?
Answer:
The six perfections are interdependently established and mutually supportive;
it is like donning armor before entering the fray—one must certainly be densely arrayed. Thus it is said.
Contemplate as one would a lamp and rest as one would in a sealed chamber.
Regarding such matters as washing clothes and cutting grass, and so forth;
furthermore, Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-realm that universally encompasses all things.
Nor is there a need for any other dharmas;
since the dharma-realm itself encompasses all dharmas,
there is likewise no need for prajñā.
Furthermore, "Prajñā is all dharmas;
all dharmas are Prajñā; they are non-dual and without distinction," and so forth.
○ Third, regarding "following one's own intention through all evil matters":
Indeed, good and evil are not fixed.
For instance, when various obscurations constitute evil deeds, their transcendence constitutes goodness;
yet when the retributions of humans and devas are exhausted, one falls back into the three miserable realms, at which point it is once again evil.
Why is this? Because both the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) and the [defiled] attainments (*samāpatti*) are by nature non-emergent and entirely evil;
whereas the emergence from suffering by the two vehicles is termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Although the practitioners of the Two Vehicles are skillful, they are only able to save themselves;
this is not the mark of a truly virtuous person.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
It would be better to give rise to the mind of a wicked,
leper-like jackal than to produce the thought of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha;
one should know that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are likewise evil.
It is praiseworthy that a Bodhisattva of the six perfections provides universal succor through both compassion and kindness; yet,
though they may provide such succor, it is like food stored in a vessel of poison— eating it will kill the person.
That which has already been abandoned is evil;
that which all three vehicles equally sever is what is called good.
Yet, failing to perceive the distinct principle, one reverts to belonging to the two extremes.
When ignorance has not yet been expelled, it is again evil;
the distinct teaching is considered good.
Although one may perceive distinct principles, as long as they still involve expedient means, they cannot be said to accord with the ultimate principle.
As the Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"Prior to this, we were all called people of wrong views."
Is the heterodox not indeed evil?
Only the Perfect Dharma is called good.
Being in accord with the true mark (dharmatā) is called the Way.
To turn one's back on the true mark (dharmatā) is called "not the Way.
If one realizes that all evils are not evil but are entirely the true mark,
then one proceeds upon what is not the Way while penetrating the Buddha-way.
If one gives rise to attachment toward the Buddha-way, the nectar will not be digested;
the Way will become a non-Way.
This principle applies universally to the discussion of good and evil.
Now, to explain good and evil specifically: in terms of phenomena,
that which accords with the [six] perfections is good,
while the various obscurations are evil.
The application of contemplation regarding wholesome phenomena has already been explained as above; the contemplation regarding unwholesome phenomena shall now be explained.
Although one previously contemplated the wholesome, their obscurations did not cease;
the afflictions were vast and pervasive, arising at all times.
If one contemplates the evils of others, they too are immeasurable.
Therefore, when cultivating the perception that all worlds are unworthy of delight,
one sees neither good people nor good lands, but only being entangled and enveloped by various obscurations and evils.
Even if they do not possess all [defilements], they may still give rise to unwholesome states in a biased manner—
such as being excessively stingy or greedy, excessively transgressing the precepts,
excessively prone to anger, excessively indolent, or excessively addicted to the taste of alcohol.
Faculties that are easily diverted will inevitably lead to faults and afflictions;
who is there who is without failure?
Even those who have left the household life and departed from the world find their practice still incomplete.
Laypeople who indulge in sensual desires are not practitioners of the Path;
evil is their lot.
Even for Arhats, there remain residual habits.
How much more so for ordinary people!
If ordinary people indulge in the obscuration of evil,
they will be crushed and cast down, never having a time of emergence.
One should cultivate contemplative wisdom even amidst evil,
just as laypeople did during the time of the Buddha,
when they lived with their wives and children.
Those engaged in official and worldly affairs can all attain the Way.
Aṅgulimāla became increasingly compassionate as he killed more people;
Jeta and Mallikā found themselves in the midst of wine yet remained solely focused on the precepts.
Vasumitra engaged in sexual misconduct yet maintained the holy life;
Devadatta held wrong views which were then rectified.
If all that is evil were invariably and exclusively evil, [these cases would not occur].
Those who cannot cultivate the Path are such people who remain forever ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*),
because there is a path even within evil.
Although one may practice amidst various obscurations and yet achieve sainthood,
we know from this that evil does not obstruct the Path,
nor does the Path obstruct evil.
In those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna, sexual desire increases;
Pindola Bharadvāja harbors pride;
and Śāriputra gives rise to anger.
What benefit or harm could there be for that which is untainted?
It is like the fact that light and darkness do not exclude one another within space; this is precisely the meaning of the manifestation of the Buddha’s bodhi.
If a person’s nature is characterized by abundant greed and defilements that burn intensely,
even though they apply remedies to subdue them, these afflictions increase all the more;
they merely indulge themselves in their pursuit.
Why is this? If obscuration does not arise, one cannot cultivate insight (vipaśyanā).
It is like a fishing line: if the hook is strong and the rope is weak, they cannot pull against one another.
Provided that the hook and bait enter the mouth, one may let it drift or sink at its own distance; before long, it will be reeled in.
Engaging in the cultivation of contemplation while remaining obscured is likewise like this.
Obscuration is like the evil fish;
contemplation is like the hook and bait.
If there were no fish, the hook and bait would be useless.
Provided that there is a fish, the larger the better;
one follows it with hook and bait, never abandoning it.
This concealment will not last long before it can be ridden and controlled.
What is contemplation?
If sensual desire arises,
one contemplates that sensual desire with its four characteristics.
Not yet covetous;
desiring to covet;
currently coveting.
Once greed has ceased,
does desire-greed arise when it has not yet ceased,
or does desire-greed arise when it has already ceased?
Desire and greed arise when they are both extinguished and not extinguished;
desire and greed arise when they are neither extinguished nor not extinguished;
or if desire arises while it has not yet been extinguished.
Whether it be identical or distinct,
if it arises immediately upon ceasing,
then arising and ceasing would be contradictory.
If it were to arise apart from [the cause],
its arising would be without a cause;
yet, if desire were to arise while craving has not yet ceased, [this would be impossible].
Are they identical or distinct?
If they are identical, then the two characteristics of arising would arise simultaneously, leading to an infinite regress.
If they are distinct, then arising itself would be without a cause.
If one desires to arise from that which is both extinguished and not extinguished:
if it arises from the extinguished, it need not also be not extinguished;
if it arises from the not extinguished, it need not also be extinguished.
How could an indeterminate cause produce a determinate effect?
If their substance were one, their natures would be contradictory;
if their substance were different, they would fundamentally be unrelated.

If desire and greed arise neither from that which is extinguished nor from that which is not extinguished, then does this state of "neither-nor" exist or not exist? If this "neither-nor" exists, how can it be called "neither-nor"?
If this "neither-nor" does not exist, how can it give rise [to desire]?
In these four propositions, one does not perceive the arising of sensual desire;
conversely, in the four propositions, one does not perceive the cessation of that which has not yet become sensual desire,
nor the arising of sensual desire.
Neither arising, nor both arising and not arising, nor neither arising nor not arising;
these are also as explained above.
Contemplate that the obscuration of craving is ultimately empty and quiescent;
illuminate both aspects with clarity,
as described above.
This is called the hook and bait.

If one constantly gives rise to this contemplation and constantly illuminates it, one neither perceives the arising nor perceives the illumination; yet there is arising and there is illumination. Furthermore, one contemplates: by what object does this obscuration arise?
Is it form, or something else?
By what cause does it arise?
Is it volitional formations, or something else?
If it is based on form,
it is either not yet seen and one desires to see it, or it has already been seen;
if it is based on formations (saṃskāra), it is likewise.
Regarding those who have not yet engaged in misconduct, those currently engaging in it, and those who have already finished engaging in it—
on account of what do they arise?
Is it for the sake of violating the precepts?
Is it for the sake of one's kinsmen?
Is it out of deception?
Or is it out of envy?
Is it for the sake of benevolence and yielding?
Is it for the sake of wholesome dhyāna?
Or is it for the sake of nirvāṇa?
Is it for the sake of the four virtues?
Is it for the sake of the six perfections or the three samādhis?
Or is it for the sake of the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges? When one contemplates in this way, there is no recipient of sensory objects.
Within conditions there is no agent;
yet, regarding objects, sensations, faculties, and conditions, they are clearly and simultaneously illumined.
Illusory transformations, emptiness, and the nature of phenomena do not obstruct one another.
Why is this? If the nature of phenomena were obscured or obstructed,
that nature would have to be subject to destruction.
If the nature of phenomena were obstructed by obscuration,
then obscuration could not arise;
one should know that obscuration is itself the nature of phenomena.
The arising of obscurations is the arising of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
the cessation of obscurations is the cessation of the nature of phenomena.
As the *Caryā-apratiprasrabdhi Sūtra* says:
Greed itself is the Way;
hatred and delusion are likewise so.
Within these three dharmas, all the Buddha-dharmas are fully contained.
If a person seeks awakening while remaining detached from desire,
it is like heaven and earth;
yet desire itself is awakening.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"To practice what is not the path is to penetrate the Buddha-way;
all sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi, which can no longer be further attained."
The characteristic of nirvana itself cannot be extinguished further.
For those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), it is said that freedom from lust, anger, and delusion is called liberation;
for those without overweening pride, it is said that the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is liberation.
All afflictions are the lineage of the Tathāgata;
the colors and flavors of mountains and seas are non-dual and without distinction.

This is precisely the contemplation of the inconceivable principle of all evils. Third, one should constantly cultivate contemplative wisdom so that it accords with the principle of subduing [afflictions].
It is like a form and its shadow;
this is called the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*).
It is capable [of renouncing] all unwholesome dharmas and worldly occupations.
All of these are not in contradiction with actual observation;
this is the stage of semblance,
wherein one enters the copper wheel and shatters the root of obscuration.
The "root" refers to ignorance;
when the root inclines and the branches break, the Buddha-nature is revealed.
This is the stage of partial realization of reality.
The ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*) is defined as the point where even the Buddhas have completely exhausted the source and depth of all obscurations.
Within the obscuration of greed, one vertically possesses the six stages of "immediacy" (*ch'ik*) and horizontally possesses the various perfections (*pāramitā*).
All dharmas are illustrated by the above examples, and so forth.
Next, observe the obscuration of anger.
If a person is full of anger, with a state of intense, surging agitation arising continuously and constantly,
such that it cannot be severed when one seeks to sever it, nor subdued when one seeks to subdue it.
One should allow the arising of illumination to proceed freely through the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One contemplates the four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] to discern from where anger arises;
if its arising cannot be found, its cessation likewise cannot be found.
Examining these twelve matters, from whom does anger arise?
Who is the one who is angry?
And who is the object of that anger?
When observing in this way, one does not give rise to anger;
the traces of coming and going,
as well as their characteristics, are empty and quiescent.
Contemplating anger through the ten dharma realms and contemplating anger through the four virtues,
as explained above in detail.
This is called attaining penetration into the Buddha-way by means of the non-way of anger.
One contemplates the obscurations of violating the precepts, indolence, distraction, and false ignorance, as well as all other such evil matters; it is the same for these four.
(4) One contemplates that which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
This refers to the indeterminate state of mental dullness and confusion.
The reason one must observe this is that there are individuals whose innate faculties are such that they neither perform wholesome deeds nor commit unwholesome ones.
Thus, there would be no following one's own intention.
Regarding such a person, what can be done about the causes and conditions for transcending the world?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
When the prajñāpāramitā is present within the indeterminate,
one immediately attains the cultivation of contemplation.
One contemplates this indeterminate state.
Are they different from or the same as the wholesome and the unwholesome?
If they were the same, they would not be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If they were different, then the determinate would cease and the indeterminate would arise.
The indeterminate arises from that which is determinate and not subject to cessation;
it also arises from that which is determinate and both subject to and not subject to cessation;
and it arises from that which is determinate and neither subject to nor not subject to cessation.
Even seeking a prediction (vyākaraṇa) is unattainable;
how much more so the identity or difference between the unpredicated (avyākṛta) and the predicted?
Since they are not identical, they do not conjoin.
Because they are not different, they do not disperse;
because they do not combine, they do not arise;
because they do not disperse, they do not cease.
Furthermore, among the twelve links, in which link does the indeterminate arise?
For what purpose does it arise?
And what is the indeterminate?
When observing in this way, it is identical to the characteristic of empty space.
Furthermore, a single indeterminate dharma gives rise to the ten dharma-realms and all phenomena.
Moreover, the indeterminate is itself the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
The eternal quiescence of the dharma-nature is the meaning of *śamatha*;
its constant illumination while in a state of quiescence is the meaning of *vipaśyanā*.
To penetrate the non-path of the indeterminate is to realize the Buddha-way.
The indeterminate (avyākṛta) constitutes the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
It encompasses all phenomena horizontally and the six stages vertically,
being complete in its height and breadth.
As stated above, furthermore,
this refers specifically to the final [category] as clearly elucidating "according to one's own intention" (svābhiprāya);
this is the intended meaning of the sequence.
If both good and evil are clearly understood as following one's own mind,
this is the sudden approach. If,
however, one relies on the gradual unfolding of goodness to clarify following one's own mind, this is the gradual approach.
"This refers to the 'unfixed mind' and so forth.
Furthermore, while the methods for the four kinds of samādhi differ from one another,
their principle of contemplation is the same."
However, the methods of the three practices mostly give rise to auxiliary dharma-gates,
which further disturb the obstacles to the Path.
Since the practice of "following one's own mind" has few such methods, it does not do so.
One initiates these matters only to a small extent;
if one merely understands the methods for initiating the aids to the path,
one will be unable to penetrate their phenomenal characteristics.
If one understands the principle but does not observe phenomena, there is nothing that will be thoroughly understood.
Furthermore, if one does not grasp the intent of observing the principle,
then even if phenomena assist one another, the Path will not be accomplished.
One attains the samādhi of the spontaneous self-perfection of principle, contemplation, mind, and phenomena.
If one enters the practice hall while practicing through phenomena, one can apply the mind;
however, upon exiting, one cannot do so.
Following one's own intention is "without interval" (nirantara).
The methods are restricted to three,
while the contemplation of principle (li-guan) applies to all four, and so forth.
Question:
The three samādhis mentioned above all include exhortations to practice;

Question:
Since the practice of the Middle Way and Right Contemplation is sufficient for unifying the mind,
why is it necessary to employ the four kinds of samādhi so elaborately?
Passing through various good and evil experiences for twelve matters—
when the water is turbid and the pearl obscured, with much wind stirring up waves—
what benefit is there in clarity and stillness?
Answer:
It is like a poor person who, having obtained a small amount,
considers it sufficient and no longer aspires to anything better.
If one contemplates the mind as being of a single nature, or if it is of various natures, what can be done?
This would constitute a failure in one's own practice.
If it were used to transform others, [the same fault would apply].
Their faculties and natures are diverse and discordant;
the afflictions of even a single person are already immeasurable,
let alone those of many.
It is like a physician who gathers all medicines to treat all diseases;
yet when a patient requires a specific medicine to cure a specific ailment,
they find it strange that the physician possesses so many medicines.
Your question is appropriate.
The mental illnesses of the afflictions are immeasurable and boundless;
as they are for one person, so it is for many.
What is the one person?
If there is a person who wishes to hear the four kinds of samādhi and hears them with joy,
one must explain them to them in their entirety.
This constitutes the world;
by hearing these four kinds of sequential practices,
one is able to give rise to wholesome dharmas.
He then explained all four;
these were for individuals respectively,
or for those who should be treated by means of constant sitting among the various evils.
Up to the point of remedying one's various evils according to one's own intention—
this is called "antidote.
Such a person must possess four dharmas.
Suddenly he attained awakening.
This is the primary truth;
yet even for a single person, it still requires fourfold teaching.
Why is it not used?
If it is for the sake of many people,
one person may prefer to sit constantly.
Third, that which is not desired:
while one person may desire to constantly practice what is not desired by others,
he universally accords with the desires of the multitude.
This is precisely the world-standpoint (loka-siddhānta).
The other three standpoints are likewise so.
Furthermore, this is also explained in terms of a single type of samādhi.
It also possesses the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*.
If one delights in walking, one walks; if one delights in sitting, one sits.
When walking, if one’s roots of goodness are brought forth, one enters into the various Dharma-gates.
At such a time one should walk;
if, while sitting, the mind-ground is cool, joyful, and at ease,
then at such a time one should sit.
If one becomes dull and drowsy while sitting, one should shake oneself off and practice walking meditation.
If one becomes distracted or fatigued while walking, then one should sit.
If one becomes vacant and tranquil while walking, [one should sit].
This is when one should walk.
If, while sitting, the mind is serene, clear, and sharp, this is when one should sit.
The other three postures are treated in the same manner, and so forth.
Question:
It is possible to cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā when one skillfully accords with principle;
but how can one cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā when one’s evil actions deviate from principle?
Answer:
The *Mahā-śāstra* clarifies that there are four types of faculties with obstructions:
first, those with sharp faculties who have no obstructions.
1. Those with sharp faculties who possess obstacles;
2. those with sharp faculties who lack obstacles; 3. those with dull faculties who lack obstacles;
4. those with dull faculties who possess obstacles.
The first phrase refers to the superior grade.
During the time of the Buddha, such as Śāriputra and others, were the individuals who practiced śamatha and vipaśyanā within the wholesome dharmas.
As for the practitioner, they cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā amidst the wholesome dharmas.
By diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas, one will face no obstacles in the future;
by constantly practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā, one’s faculties are made sharp.
If one possessed these two meanings in the past, [the result follows].
If one practices even slightly in this life, one immediately attains correspondence and enters the stage of semblance-reality from the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
As for those who do not enter it in this life, there is no meaning of "past" [in their case], as they have never been without the two [aspects].
Now, based on those who have practiced well, they will swiftly enter [the path] in the future.
As for the next category, their roots for attaining the Way are sharp, yet their accumulated offenses and heavy obstacles remain;
such were King Ajātaśatru and Aṅgulimāla during the time of the Buddha.
This illustrates the person concerned:
though their obstructive sins were grave enough to warrant entry into hell,
upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, they suddenly and completely attained sainthood.
Because their faculties are sharp, they are shielded from what cannot be obstructed;
this is precisely the meaning intended when practitioners nowadays cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā amidst unwholesome dharmas.
Because evil has arisen, there will be obstacles in the future;
because one has cultivated śamatha and vipaśyanā, one's faculties will be sharp in subsequent lives.
If one encounters a spiritual friend, they will spur one on to enter the right path.
Why do you say that those who harbor evil dharmas and act contrary to principle are unwilling to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
Next, regarding those with dull faculties who are without obstruction:
In the time of the Buddha, Cūḍapanthaka was shown to be that very person;
although his three karmas were without fault, his innate faculties were extremely dull.
For ninety days, he recited the verses of Kumārajīva.
The Wise One did not commit any evil through body, speech, or mind;
with mindfulness constantly present before him, he took no pleasure in or became attached to any desires.
Nor do they undergo the world’s useless ascetic practices.
Although they maintain the precepts and perform wholesome deeds in the present, they do not study *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Consequently, in the future, though there will be no obstacles, it will be extremely difficult for them to realize the Way.
The latter phrase refers to those who perform all manner of evil deeds,
as well as those who do not cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Because they do not cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they do not attain the Way.
With dull faculties, even if one explains it to them a thousand times, they remain utterly without understanding;
they commit many evil deeds and create myriad kinds of obstructions.
It is like a person with leprosy whose body is numb; even when needles pierce to the bone, they feel nothing and remain unaware.
They merely entangle themselves with various evils.
For this reason, [it is said].
Although goodness supports the Way through the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*,
and although evil opposes the principle through sharp faculties that break down obstructions,
only the Way is supreme.
How could one abandon contemplation and insight on account of committing evil?

"To be lax regarding the precepts is not what is meant by being lax."
That which is lax regarding the vehicle is what is called "laxity.

Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
"It would be better to be Devadatta than to be Udraka Rāmaputra"—

If one practices in accordance with the Middle Way, there will be a supreme and wondrous retribution;
even if one has not yet transcended the realm of分段 (fen-duan,
limited分段 birth), the provisional rewards obtained will also differ from those of the seven types of expedient means.
How much more so for the true karmic fruition!
The sevenfold bridges and ferries of the City of Fragrance are like a painting;
this is precisely their characteristic appearance. This meaning will be explained later in the eighth section.

Question:
The *Cidi Chanmen* (The Sequential Gate of Dhyāna) clarifies cultivation and realization.
How does this differ from its karmic retribution?
Answer:
"Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to habitual practice, while "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) refers to the attainment through manifestation.
Furthermore, "cultivation" refers to the cause of habituation and "realization" refers to the fruit of habituation;
both can be obtained within this very life.
However, the present treatise discusses the retribution of the realms, which is separated from the present and occurs in future lives.
This is what distinguishes them.
In the Two Vehicles, there are only the fruits of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*) and no fruits of retribution (*vipāka-phala*);
in the Mahāyāna, both are fully present, and so forth.
The fourth reason for teaching this śamatha-vipaśyanā is to penetrate the great net of various sūtras and śāstras.
If a person skillfully employs śamatha-vipaśyanā to contemplate the mind, [they will realize the truth].
Thus, with internal wisdom clearly illuminated,
one penetrates all gradual and sudden teachings,
like extracting a great thousand-fold sutra from a shattered atom of dust.
The Buddha-dharma, vast as the sands of the Ganges, is realized within a single moment of mind.
If one wishes to benefit sentient beings externally by establishing teachings according to their capacities,
one speaks in accordance with what each person is able to receive.
Until the time he attains Buddhahood and transforms sentient beings,
he may act as a Dharma King to preach the sudden and gradual teachings,
or he may act as a Bodhisattva.
Sometimes he manifests as the forms of beings within the ten dharma realms—such as śrāvakas, celestial māras, humans, or ghosts—to inspire and provoke [realization].
Sometimes he answers at length, whether gradually or suddenly, to questions posed by the Buddha.
Or he may pose questions to the Buddha to test his capacity.
The Buddha’s response concerning the sudden and gradual wheels of Dharma will be explained in detail in the ninth section;
it is also briefly indicated within the "Compendium of Teachings" (*Shèfǎ*).
Fifth, regarding the taking refuge in the Great State: because all phenomena are ultimately empty, this is called the teaching of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Now, it is said that when glue sticks to the hand, it is easy to remove, but when one is dreaming in sleep, it is difficult to awaken.
Feng Wenqi’s mind was so set on his own views that he considered them to be correct;
he vied with others to grasp tiles and pebbles, calling them lapis lazuli beads.
Even regarding recent events and plain speech, he still fails to recognize them.
How much more so regarding the distant principles and the esoteric teachings—how could one not be confused?
For this reason, it is necessary to discuss the ultimate aim (*zhiguī*).
"Ultimate aim" refers to the direction toward which the meaning of the text tends.
Like water flowing toward the sea or a flame rising toward the sky,
consciousness penetrates to the far reaches without obstruction.
It is like a wise minister who understands the king’s secret speech.
Upon hearing whatever is taught, they fully comprehend it and reach the stage of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
One who attains this intention understands the ultimate purpose.
As for that "purpose," it is to direct oneself toward the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
"Returning" (gui) means leading others to enter together into the Three Virtues;
thus it is called the "Ultimate Return" (zhigui).
Furthermore, entering the Three Virtues oneself is called "returning" (gui).
To cause others to enter the meaning of the Three Virtues is called the "Ultimate Goal" (zhìguī).
Thus it is named the Ultimate Goal.
Now, I shall further clarify this ultimate goal both collectively and individually.
The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition.
They manifest various forms,
causing all sentient beings alike to perceive the Dharma-body.
Having seen the Dharma-body,
both the Buddha and sentient beings together return to the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, the Buddha preaches various dharmas.
May all sentient beings ultimately attain the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.
Once this knowledge of all modes is perfected,
both the Buddha and sentient beings shall together return to Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, the Buddha manifests various skillful means, supernatural powers, and transformations to liberate all from their bonds,
not allowing even a single person to attain extinction alone,
but rather causing them all to attain extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
Once they have entered parinirvāṇa,
both the Buddha and sentient beings together return to liberation.
As the Great Sūtra says:
I shall place all my children within the secret treasury,
and before long, I myself shall abide therein as well.
This is called the general characteristic of the ultimate destination.
Regarding distinct characteristics, the body is of three kinds:
first, the form-body;
second, the dharma-gate body.
Third is the body of true reality (*dharmatā-kāya*).
If one ceases the discussion of transformation and returns [to the source],
the form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) returns to liberation.
The body of the Dharma-gate returns to Prajñā;
the body of true reality returns to the Dharmakāya.
Regarding Prajñā, three types are taught.
First, it speaks of the knowledge of the paths;
second, it speaks of all-knowledge;
third, it speaks of the knowledge of all aspects.
If one returns from the discourse on transformation,
the knowledge of the modes of the path returns to liberation;
the knowledge of all things returns to prajñā.
The knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is subsumed within the dharma-body (dharmakāya).
There are three kinds of liberation:
first, liberation from the bondage of ignorance.
Second, liberation from the bondage of grasping at signs;
third, liberation from the bondage of ignorance.
If transformation ceases and one returns to the Real, [these bondages are severed].
To untie the bond of ignorance is to return to liberation;
to untie the bond of grasping at signs is to return to prajñā;
to untie the bond of nescience is to return to the dharmakāya.
For this reason, the ultimate aim of the distinct characteristics also converges within the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Furthermore, these three virtues are neither three nor one; they are inconceivable.
Why is this? If one were to say that the Dharma-body is merely the Dharma-body,
it would not be the Dharma-body.
One should know that the Dharma-body is also a body, yet not a body; it is neither a body nor a non-body.
Abiding in Śūraṅgama-samādhi, it manifests in various ways, assuming all manner of forms and images.
Therefore it is called the body.
Having accomplished what was to be done, one returns to liberation.
Wisdom clearly illuminates all that is material and non-material.
Therefore, it is called "non-body.
Having accomplished what was to be done, one returns to Prajñā.
This body of true reality is neither a body of form and appearance nor a body of the Dharma-gate.
Therefore, it is neither body nor non-body.
Having accomplished what was to be done, one returns to the Dharma-body.
To realize that these three bodies possess no characteristic of either unity or difference is called "returning."
To say that these three bodies possess neither the characteristic of unity nor difference is what is called the "Essential Meaning" (zhì).
Because all enter together into the secret treasury, it is named the "Ultimate Destination" (zhìguī).
If one were to say that what is directly called "prajñā" is not prajñā,
one should know that prajñā also knows that it is neither knowing nor non-knowing, nor is it the negation of non-knowing.
Because the prajñā of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) universally cognizes the conventional, it is termed "knowing."
Having accomplished what was to be done, one returns to liberation;
because omniscient prajñā thoroughly knows reality, it is called "non-knowing.
Having accomplished what was to be done, one returns to prajñā.
The prajñā of the knowledge of all modes thoroughly knows within this;
therefore, it is called neither knowing nor not knowing.
Having accomplished what was to be done, it returns to the dharmakāya.
To realize that the three types of *prajñā* possess neither the characteristic of unity nor the characteristic of difference is called "taking refuge.
To explain that the three types of *prajñā* possess neither the characteristic of unity nor the characteristic of difference is [the meaning of taking refuge].
This is what is meant by "the intent.
Because they both enter the secret treasury, it is called the "ultimate resort.
If one were to say that liberation is simply liberation, [it would be incomplete].
It is not liberation. You should know that liberation is also free from being liberated, free from not being liberated, and free from neither being liberated nor not being liberated.
Through skillful means, it purifies liberation and subdues sentient beings without being defiled by them.
Therefore, it is called "liberation.
Having accomplished what was to be done, one returns to liberation;
because this perfectly pure liberation does not perceive sentient beings nor the characteristics of liberation, it is called "non-liberation."
Once what was to be done has been accomplished, one returns to prajñā.
Since its nature is pure liberation, it is neither liberated nor non-liberated.
Once what was to be done has been accomplished, one returns to the dharmakāya.
Whether it be realization or exposition,
these three liberations do not possess the characteristics of being either identical or distinct;
because they all enter the secret treasury, they are called the "Ultimate Goal."
Furthermore, the three virtues (triguṇa) are neither new nor old, yet they are both new and old.
Why is this? Because the three obstructions (trisaṃkleśa) obstruct the three virtues.
Ignorance obstructs the dharmakāya;
grasping at signs obstructs prajñā;
lack of knowledge obstructs liberation.
The three obstacles (trivaraṇa) are called "old" because they existed previously;
the three virtues (triguṇa) are called "new" because they are now first manifested through the destruction of those three obstacles.
The three obstacles are the three virtues, and the three virtues are the three obstacles.
The three obstacles are the three virtues because the three obstacles are not old;
the three virtues are the three obstacles because the three virtues are not new.
That which is not new yet appears new consists of the three virtues attained through the arousal of the bodhicitta,
up to the three virtues attained at the ultimate stage;
that which is not old yet appears old consists of the three obstacles to be remediated by the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Even unto the ultimate three obstacles to be remedied—
being neither new nor old, neither ancient nor recent—

there exist the three virtues of the rational nature (tathatā-gotra). If one comprehensively realizes that these three virtues are neither new nor old, yet are both new and old, [the obstacles are transcended].
There is no characteristic of identity or difference; it is likewise for others.
This is precisely the ultimate destination within the Secret Treasury.
Furthermore, it is said that because that which existed prior to ignorance is called "old," while the Dharmakāya—
which is clarity that destroys ignorance— is called "new."
Ignorance is itself clarity, and clarity is itself ignorance;
for ignorance is not something that existed prior to clarity, and clarity is not something newly produced after ignorance.
Ignorance is itself clarity, and thus clarity is not something new.
Grasping at marks is called "old" because it precedes [the realization of] names;
the absence of marks and the destruction of marks is called "new.
Marks are themselves the absence of marks, and the absence of marks is itself marks.
What is "new" and for what reason?
Ignorance (ajñāna) existing first is termed the "old.
Knowledge (jñāna) that destroys ignorance is termed the "new."
Non-knowing is itself knowing, and knowing is itself non-knowing.
What is new? What is the reason?
If one penetrates both the general and the particular, there is not a single characteristic of newness or antiquity, nor of identity or difference.
If one explains it to others, it is likewise so.
This is called the ultimate destination for entering the Secret Treasury.
Whether opening or closing, whether proceeding from beginning to end or vice versa, all such examples are like this.
Furthermore, the ultimate destination is likewise thus:
the destination is not the destination, nor is it not the destination, nor is it neither the destination nor not the destination;
the returning is not the returning, nor is it not the returning, nor is it neither the returning nor not the returning.
Each and every one must enter into the Secret Treasury;
this can be understood by analogy with what precedes,
as its purport pertains to one's own practice.
It is not for the purpose of transforming others;
it is neither a purpose nor a non-purpose, as there is no distinction between self and other.
Such is the peaceful stillness of the ultimate return to the Three Virtues.
What name could possibly be used to describe it?
Not knowing how to name it, one forcibly designates it as "the Middle Way," "the True Mark," "the Dharma-body," "neither cessation nor contemplation," and so forth.
Furthermore, they are also forcibly designated as "all-aspect wisdom," "equal great prajñā," "perfection of wisdom," "contemplation," and so forth;
they are also forcibly designated as "śūraṅgama samādhi," "great nirvāṇa," "inconceivable liberation," "cessation," and so forth.
One should know that various characteristics, various teachings, and various supernormal powers—
all of these individually enter into the Secret Treasury.
What is this ultimate destination?
Where is the ultimate destination?
Who is it that reaches this destination?
It is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Permanently quiescent like space—
this is called the ultimate refuge.
This shall be explained in detail in the tenth section.
Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā, Fascicle Two, Part Two.
